{{Short description|Vector field defined for any energy function}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[physics]], a '''Hamiltonian vector field''' on a [[symplectic manifold]] is a [[vector field]] defined for any '''energy function''' or '''Hamiltonian'''. Named after the physicist and mathematician [[William Rowan Hamilton|Sir William Rowan Hamilton]], a Hamiltonian vector field is a geometric manifestation of [[Hamilton's equations]] in [[classical mechanics]]. The [[integral curve]]s of a Hamiltonian vector field represent solutions to the [[equations of motion]] in the Hamiltonian form. The [[diffeomorphism]]s of a symplectic manifold arising from the [[flow (mathematics)|flow]] of a Hamiltonian vector field are known as [[canonical transformation]]s in physics and (Hamiltonian) [[symplectomorphism]]s in mathematics.{{sfn|Lee|2003|loc=Chapter 18}}

Hamiltonian vector fields can be defined more generally on an arbitrary [[Poisson manifold]]. The [[Lie bracket of vector fields|Lie bracket]] of two Hamiltonian vector fields corresponding to functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> on the manifold is itself a Hamiltonian vector field, with the Hamiltonian given by the [[Poisson bracket]] of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>.

== Definition ==
Suppose that <math>(M,\omega)</math> is a [[symplectic manifold]]. Since the [[Symplectic manifold|symplectic form]] <math>\omega</math> is nondegenerate, it sets up a ''fiberwise-linear'' [[isomorphism]]

<math display="block">\omega: TM \to T^*M, </math>

between the [[tangent bundle]] <math>TM</math> and the [[cotangent bundle]] <math>T^*M</math>, with the inverse

<math display="block">\Omega: T^* M \to T M, \quad \Omega = \omega^{-1}.</math>

Therefore, [[one-form]]s on a symplectic manifold <math>M</math> may be identified with [[vector field]]s and every [[differentiable function]] <math>H:M\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> determines a unique [[vector field]] <math>X_H</math>, called the ''Hamiltonian vector field'' with the ''Hamiltonian'' <math>H</math>, by defining for every vector field <math>Y</math> on <math>M</math>,

<math display="block">\mathrm{d}H(Y) = \omega(X_H,Y).</math>Or more succinctly, <math>\iota_{X_H} \omega = dH</math>.

'''Note''': Some authors define the Hamiltonian vector field with the opposite sign. One has to be mindful of varying conventions in physical and mathematical literature.

== Examples ==
Suppose that <math>M</math> is a <math>2n</math>-dimensional symplectic manifold. Then locally, one may choose [[canonical coordinates]] <math>(q^1,\cdots,q^n,p_1,\cdots,p_n)</math> on <math>M</math>, in which the symplectic form is expressed as:{{sfn|Lee|2003|loc=Chapter 12}} <math>\omega = \sum_i \mathrm{d}q^i \wedge \mathrm{d}p_i,</math>

where <math>\operatorname{d}</math> denotes the [[exterior derivative]] and <math>\wedge</math> denotes the [[exterior product]]. Then the Hamiltonian vector field with Hamiltonian <math>H</math> takes the form:{{sfn|Lee|2003|loc=Chapter 18}} <math>\Chi_H = \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i},
- \frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i} \right) = \Omega\,\mathrm{d}H,</math>

where <math>\Omega</math> is a <math>2n\times 2n</math> square matrix

<math display="block">\Omega =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & I_n \\
-I_n & 0 \\
\end{bmatrix},</math>

and

<math display="block"> \mathrm{d}H = \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i} \\
\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}
\end{bmatrix}.</math>

The matrix <math>\Omega</math> is frequently denoted with <math>\mathbf{J}</math>.

Suppose that <math>M=\mathbb{R}^{2n}</math> is the <math>2n</math>-dimensional [[symplectic vector space]] with (global) canonical coordinates.

* If <math>H = p_i</math> then <math>X_H = \partial/\partial q^i; </math>
* if <math>H = q_i</math> then <math>X_H = -\partial/\partial p^i; </math>
* if <math display="inline">H = \frac{1}{2} \sum (p_i)^2</math> then <math display="inline">X_H = \sum p_i\partial/\partial q^i; </math>
* if <math display="inline">H = \frac{1}{2} \sum a_{ij} q^i q^j, a_{ij} = a_{ji} </math> then <math display="inline">X_H = -\sum a_{ij} q_i\partial/\partial p^j. </math>

== Properties ==
* The assignment <math>f\mapsto X_f</math> is [[linear map|linear]], so that the sum of two Hamiltonian functions transforms into the sum of the corresponding Hamiltonian vector fields.
* Suppose that <math>(q^1,\cdots,q^n,p_1,\cdots,p_n)</math> are canonical coordinates on <math>M</math> (see above). Then a curve <math>\gamma(t)=(q(t),p(t))</math> is an [[integral curve]] of the Hamiltonian vector field <math>X_H</math> [[if and only if]] it is a solution of [[Hamilton's equations]]:{{sfn|Lee|2003|loc=Chapter 18}} <math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot{q}^i & = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} \\
\dot{p}_i & =-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}.
\end{align}</math>
* The Hamiltonian <math>H</math> is constant along the integral curves, because <math>\langle dH, \dot{\gamma}\rangle = \omega(X_H(\gamma),X_H(\gamma)) = 0</math>. That is, <math>H(\gamma(t))</math> is actually independent of <math>t</math>. This property corresponds to the [[conservation of energy]] in [[Hamiltonian mechanics]].
* More generally, if two functions <math>F</math> and <math>H</math> have a zero [[Poisson bracket]] (cf. below), then <math>F</math> is constant along the integral curves of <math>H</math>, and similarly, <math>H</math> is constant along the integral curves of <math>F</math>. This fact is the abstract mathematical principle behind [[Noether's theorem]].<ref group=nb>See {{harvtxt|Lee|2003|loc=Chapter 18}} for a very concise statement and proof of Noether's theorem.</ref>
* The [[Symplectic manifold|symplectic form]] <math>\omega</math> is preserved by the Hamiltonian flow. Equivalently, the [[Lie derivative]] <math>\mathcal{L}_{X_H} \omega=0</math>.

==Poisson bracket==
The notion of a Hamiltonian vector field leads to a [[Bilinear form#Symmetric, skew-symmetric and alternating forms|skew-symmetric]] bilinear operation on the differentiable functions on a symplectic manifold <math>M</math>, the '''[[Poisson bracket]]''', defined by the formula

<math display="block">\{f,g\} = \omega(X_g, X_f)= dg(X_f) = \mathcal{L}_{X_f} g</math>

where <math>\mathcal{L}_X</math> denotes the [[Lie derivative]] along a vector field <math>X</math>. Moreover, one can check that the following identity holds:{{sfn|Lee|2003|loc=Chapter 18}} <math> X_{\{f,g\}}= -[X_f,X_g]</math>,

where the right hand side represents the Lie bracket of the Hamiltonian vector fields with Hamiltonians <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>. As a consequence (a proof at [[Poisson bracket]]), the Poisson bracket satisfies the [[Jacobi identity]]:{{sfn|Lee|2003|loc=Chapter 18}} <math> \{\{f,g\},h\} + \{\{g,h\},f\} + \{\{h,f\},g\}=0</math>,

which means that the vector space of differentiable functions on <math>M</math>, endowed with the Poisson bracket, has the structure of a [[Lie algebra]] over <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, and the assignment <math>f\mapsto X_f</math> is a [[Lie algebra homomorphism]], whose [[kernel (linear algebra)|kernel]] consists of the locally constant functions (constant functions if <math>M</math> is connected).
